## Which suits your child?

| Factor | Private lesson | Group lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Instructor attention | Fully one-to-one; pace and drills can be tailored each minute | Shared attention; progress follows the group’s lesson structure |
| Best for | Water anxiety, beginners who need confidence, neurodivergent learners, stroke correction, catching up before camp or vacation | Children who enjoy peers, are generally comfortable in water, and benefit from routine and social motivation |
| Learning pace | Usually faster for a specific objective, assuming regular practice | Often steadier; children may learn through watching peers and repeated class routines |
| Social experience | Minimal peer interaction | Builds comfort participating with others and can make lessons more fun |
| Cost | Highest per lesson | Usually the most cost-effective option |
| Potential drawback | Can feel intense or create dependence on one instructor | Less individual feedback and potentially less flexible pacing |

Vaughan lists semi-private lessons for ages 3+ alongside private lessons. [vaughan](https://www.vaughan.ca/residential/recreation-programs-and-fitness/swimming/learn-swim)

## When private is worth it

Private lessons are most worthwhile if your child:

- Cries, freezes, or refuses to participate in a group setting.
- Has had little progress after one or two properly level-matched group sessions.
- Needs focused work on a specific skill, such as floating independently, breathing, front crawl, or deep-water confidence.
- Has a learning, sensory, communication, or mobility need that benefits from an adapted pace.
- Needs a short intensive boost before summer camp, a trip, or a school swimming requirement.

If the issue is only that they are shy on day one, I would usually give a small group class a few lessons before switching. Adjustment is common, and peer modeling can help.

## Best-value path

For a typical water-comfortable child aged 4–10:

1. Enrol in a correctly levelled group class for a full session.
2. Watch whether they receive enough corrections and are progressing in confidence—not only whether they “pass” a level.
3. Add two to four private lessons if they stall on one important skill.
4. Return to group classes to keep practicing, gain endurance, and enjoy peers.

That hybrid approach often gives the best balance of safety skills, confidence, social learning, and cost.

## When private is worth it

Private instruction is especially useful if your child:

- Is fearful of submerging, floating, or swimming without flotation.
- Has repeated the same group level without mastering a particular skill.
- Needs focused help with breathing, front crawl, deep-water confidence, or a swim-test deadline.
- Benefits from lower-stimulation, one-on-one teaching.
- Has a schedule that makes regular group offerings impractical.

For example, a child who can kick and float but panics during unassisted back floats may make better early progress in several private sessions, then transition to group lessons for repetition and peer practice.

## When a swim school is better

Choose a swim school or municipal group program if your child is generally comfortable in water, can follow a teacher in a group, and needs steady exposure rather than intensive remediation. Small-group schools can be a middle ground: more structure and consistency than many public programs, but more social practice and lower cost than 1:1.

## What matters more than format

The strongest safety signals are:

- A **low instructor-to-child ratio**. Water Safety USA recommends 1:4 or fewer for young or beginner swimmers without a caregiver in the water, and no more than 1:6. [watersafetyusa](https://www.watersafetyusa.org/what-to-look-for-in-a-learn-to-swim-program.html)
- A qualified instructor plus a **separate, actively scanning lifeguard**—not an instructor expected to teach and provide full-pool surveillance at the same time. [watersafetyusa](https://www.watersafetyusa.org/what-to-look-for-in-a-learn-to-swim-program.html)
- Children grouped by **actual ability**, not only by age. [watersafetyusa](https://www.watersafetyusa.org/what-to-look-for-in-a-learn-to-swim-program.html)
- Clear policies for missed skills, water fear, bathroom breaks, illness, and emergency response.
- Your child is supervised closely outside lessons too. Lessons help, but they do not replace touch supervision and barriers such as fences or locked pool access. [watersafetyusa](https://www.watersafetyusa.org/what-to-look-for-in-a-learn-to-swim-program.html)

## When private lessons are preferable

Consider private or semi-private instruction if your child:

- Is a non-swimmer, very young, highly fearful, or easily distracted
- Has developmental, sensory, behavioral, or medical needs requiring customized pacing
- Needs concentrated work on a particular safety skill, such as floating, rolling to the back, or reaching an exit
- Is not getting enough turns or attention in their current group

## When group lessons are a good choice

A small, well-supervised group can be appropriate if your child is comfortable in water, placed at the right skill level, and the program keeps ratios low. Group settings also give children chances to observe peers, practice waiting and listening, and become comfortable around other swimmers. Some programs use groups of about 3–4 swimmers per instructor; actual ratios vary by provider and age level. [safesplash](https://www.safesplash.com/blog/group-vs-private-swim-lessons-for-kids)

## Practical choice

If you can afford it, a useful middle ground is **semi-private instruction**—two children of similar ability with one instructor. It preserves much of the individual attention while allowing social learning.

## When private lessons win

A qualified instructor can watch what your body is actually doing—breathing timing, head position, balance, kick, and arm path—and correct one problem at a time. That immediate, individualized feedback is difficult to get from a video.

Private lessons are particularly worthwhile if you:

- Cannot yet float, tread water, or comfortably put your face in the water.
- Have a fear of deep water or a past negative experience.
- Want to learn efficiently for a trip, fitness goal, triathlon, or swim test.
- Have plateaued with a specific stroke.
- Need accommodations for an injury, disability, or strong anxiety.
- Want water-safety skills alongside strokes.

Formal learn-to-swim programs are structured around both swimming skills and water safety, with trained instructors and progression across ability levels. [redcross](https://www.redcross.org/take-a-class/swimming)

## When videos can work

Learning with videos can be reasonable if you already have basic water comfort and can practice in a safe, supervised pool. They are useful for:

- Seeing a drill before trying it.
- Reviewing cues such as “exhale underwater” or “look down, not forward.”
- Building a practice plan between lessons.
- Improving a familiar stroke after someone has already shown you the fundamentals.
- Saving money if you can get occasional technique feedback elsewhere.

The limitation is that you may not notice mistakes. For example, a video may tell you to keep your hips high in freestyle, but without external feedback you might lift your head to breathe, causing your hips to sink and reinforcing the exact issue you are trying to solve.

## Best value: a hybrid approach

For most adults, the best cost-to-progress balance is:

1. Take a short block of private lessons—such as 3–6 sessions.
2. Ask the instructor for 2–3 specific drills to practice.
3. Use videos only to review those drills.
4. Practice once or twice weekly in a pool with lifeguards or another competent swimmer present.
5. Book another lesson after a few practices to correct habits before they become ingrained.

This preserves the benefits of personalized coaching while reducing the number of paid sessions you need.

## Before the instructor arrives

- Confirm the lesson time, swimmer’s age/ability, goals, medical or allergy information, and whether the instructor supplies items such as flotation aids or toys.
- Make sure the pool is clean, clear, and at a comfortable temperature; the pump/filter should be operating normally.

- Unlock the appropriate entry route and ensure the instructor can easily access the pool area, restroom, and a place to set belongings.
- Keep pets and nonparticipating children away from the pool area during the lesson.
- Tell the instructor about pool depth, steps, ladders, deep-end transitions, diving restrictions, drains, and any equipment that could affect the lesson.

## Safety essentials

- Keep a charged phone within reach and have your full home address ready for an emergency call.
- Have a first-aid kit plus rescue equipment such as a reaching pole and ring buoy available.
- Check that drain covers are intact and teach swimmers not to play near drains or suction outlets. [poolsafely](https://www.poolsafely.gov/)
- Keep gates secured when not actively entering or leaving the area; four-sided barriers and self-closing, self-latching gates are recommended layers of protection for home pools. [redcross](https://www.redcross.org/get-help/how-to-prepare-for-emergencies/types-of-emergencies/water-safety/home-pool-safety.html)
- Designate an adult to be the undistracted “water watcher,” especially for young or inexperienced swimmers. The instructor leads the lesson, but a parent/guardian should remain on site unless you and the instructor explicitly agree otherwise. [redcross](https://www.redcross.org/get-help/how-to-prepare-for-emergencies/types-of-emergencies/water-safety/swim-safety.html)
- Have a clear rule of **no diving** unless the pool has a designated safe diving area. [redcross](https://www.redcross.org/get-help/how-to-prepare-for-emergencies/types-of-emergencies/water-safety/home-pool-safety.html)
